title: Contract Debugging
story: A team spent hours chasing a bug that manifested as 'unexpected NaN in calculation.' When they enabled runtime contracts, the error appeared instantly at the source: 'Contract violation: divisor != 0 at math.xi:42'. Twelve hours of debugging reduced to two seconds.
why: Contract violations produce precise, actionable error messages that pinpoint the exact precondition failure — turning mystery crashes into instant diagnoses.
analogy: Contract violations are like a surgeon's scalpel — they make a precise incision exactly where the problem is, instead of leaving you to diagnose symptoms.
try_it: Deliberately break a contract: create a `Temperature{ celsius: -300.0 }` and observe the error message. Then create a Stack and call `pop()` without pushing anything first. Notice how the error messages differ between invariant violations and requires violations. Which gives you more context?
tips: Always read the full contract violation trace — the call stack tells you WHICH CALLER violated the contract
Invariant violations tell you the field values at failure — use this to trace how the bad state was reached
Enable runtime contracts during development — the overhead is worth the instant bug detection
common_mistakes: Ignoring contract violation output and adding print statements instead — the output already tells you everything
Not reading the location field — 'main.xi:10' tells you exactly which line to fix
Disabling contracts in development because they 'slow things down' — the slowdown is negligible compared to debugging time saved
